title: Endgame and Live Content
summary: Defines post-story goals, recurring challenges, content cadence and live-service boundaries for long-term play.
sourceFile: Game Design/14 - Endgame and Live Content.docx

headings.text: Rule 6. Do Not Sell the Solution Immediately

blocks.text: Post-story content and ongoing live operations
The Endgame of Symphony of Justice begins once the player no longer needs to learn the core systems and starts pursuing:
MASTER → EXPERIMENT → COMPLETE → DISCOVER → COMPETE → EXPRESS
There should not be a single definition of “finishing the game.” A veteran player may continue for different reasons.
It represents the primary mechanical goal. The player seeks to:
master dodges, cooldowns, and timing windows;
Endgame progression should depend less and less on: having +500 ATK
and increasingly on: understanding when, how, and why to use what the player already has.
This aligns with the current vision that future depth should emerge through new interactions, conditions, and enemies, rather than simply increasing HP and damage.
A veteran player should have reasons to develop more than four characters. The Endgame can encourage:
The goal is for the entire roster to remain useful.
We do not want: “I have 60 characters, but I only use four.”
We want: “This challenge makes me reconsider characters I do not normally use.”

However, completing the collection should be a personal goal, not a requirement for accessing the Endgame. The Game Vision already establishes that characters should provide both gameplay and narrative value, and that obtaining them should broaden perspectives and team-building possibilities.
Endgame does not mean: the story is over. Veteran players can continue receiving:
The long-term vision already includes narrative content distributed across chapters, characters, regions, and temporary events.
For interested players, there may be:
if the competitive system is ultimately approved. However, ranking must remain optional. Players should not feel that progression necessarily means competing against others.
In the long term, Kingdomless Island can provide goals related to:
The Game Vision already considers the Island as a potential Social Hub with cooperation and community activities.
Veteran players also need ways to showcase their journey. They can do so through:
Not every Endgame reward needs to increase power.
Repeatable content should present different problems, not merely rewards that force players to repeat exactly the same activity. Historical documentation already supports:
I propose structuring it into five families.
The historical Weekly Bosses category already exists, with examples such as:
The Dragon of the Phantom Souls;
Advanced rewards may have weekly limits, but attempts should remain available.

This category is also directly documented. The historical source describes them as progressive, labyrinthine runs with elemental or regional themes and increasing difficulty. A modern version can vary through:
It can consist of a series of encounters through which the player progresses. Conceptual example:

This is not historically defined either.
The advantage is that it can reuse:
to create different runs. However, it should only be built after the core combat system works perfectly.
It allows players to fight several known Bosses sequentially. It can use:
It is relatively content-efficient because it reuses existing Bosses within a new structure.
They can be larger-scale cooperative encounters. However, they require:
Therefore, they do not belong in initial production.
Each mode should prioritize something different.
This prevents us from having six activities that are really just: “kill enemies for eight minutes.”
Events are temporary content designed to introduce: NARRATIVE + VARIATION + REWARD + EXPERIMENTATION
The historical source explicitly establishes the intent to design one special event per update and use these events to vary mechanics and avoid monotony.
The documentation does not establish an exact duration. As an initial operational target, I propose:
Not all events need to affect the main plot.
Each event should introduce at least:
It does not need to introduce a massive new system.
It should be archived after the event. We do not want a player who arrives two years later to ask: “Why are these two nations allies now?”
and the answer to be: “That was explained in a fifteen-day event in 2027.”
Therefore, narratively relevant content should be moved to:
Temporary currency can allow players to choose rewards. This provides control and reduces RNG.
An event should not add a second workday on top of:
Its activities can also grant progress toward recurring systems.
I would use the primary term:

instead of relying exclusively on “seasons.” Historical documentation already refers to content being added through versions/updates. A season may exist within competitive systems or LiveOps, but the game’s overall expansion should be organized by versions.
A version can introduce a combination of:
It does not need to include everything at the same time.
The following elements should remain persistent:
Temporary content should complement the permanent foundation.
New region, major chapter, or large-scale system.
The source does not define a release cadence, and it would be risky to establish one without knowing the team’s capacity.
when production, narrative, and art are ready. Not every X months out of obligation. The final cadence will depend on:
If PvP or ranking is later introduced: Season ≠ Game Version.
A season can span multiple versions. This prevents competitive balance and narrative production from being tied to the same calendar.
This point is fundamental to the project’s viability. A multi-year vision only works if content can be produced through a repeatable pipeline, instead of rebuilding every system from scratch.
They are among the most expensive pieces of content.
High cost, although lower than a complete region.
Reuse does not mean copying content. It means using existing systems to produce new configurations.
They can reuse existing regions while changing:
They use world content with different objectives.
The Live team should not be building the version scheduled to release next week.
Ideally, several versions should exist at different stages:
The number will depend on the actual size of the team.
That is why the cost of a Live Service does not end when an asset enters Unreal.
To sustain years of content, we will eventually need data-driven tools for:
The more a designer can configure through data without modifying code, the more sustainable LiveOps becomes.

This point already has a fairly clear direction within the Game Vision: new characters should expand possibilities, create synergies, or reinterpret existing systems, rather than relying solely on being statistically superior.
It occurs when a new character causes an older one to lose virtually every reason to exist.
With no downside. That does not expand the roster. It replaces it.
Each character should have a specific reason to be used. They may excel at:
teams built around a specific profession.
The new character may occupy the same role, but solve a different problem.
Not every new unit needs to be an: Upgrade.
Character C: lower personal damage but better reactions.
An excellent way to revitalize older characters is to introduce:
This creates: retrospective value. A character can become interesting again without directly modifying their kit.
If every Boss asks: “Who deals the most DPS?”
the character with the highest damage always wins. Instead, enemies can demand:
This preserves the value of different kits.
Only when there is a real problem. We should not constantly redesign characters. Players need to trust that what they have learned will remain recognizable.
Rule 6. Do Not Sell the Solution Immediately
A new Boss should not be designed around: “This is unbearable unless you pull for the character from this version.”

Featured characters may have natural advantages in current content. However, alternatives must always exist. This already aligns with the Game Pillars, which do not allow a battle to strictly require a specific character obtained through Gacha.
The Legacy Card can expand possibilities. However: Legacy VI should not turn a character into an entirely different power category compared with Legacy 0. This is especially important for:
Early progression can be vertical: higher numbers.
The Endgame should become increasingly horizontal: more options.
How many players immediately abandon an older unit when a new one appears.
How long a character remains useful.
Number of different team compositions that clear a challenge.
If 90% of players use exactly the same four characters, we have a problem.
